newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Clintons prepare for fun on the Great Barrier Reef.
newsitem.headline: Clintons prepare for fun on the Great Barrier Reef.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton, fresh from a round of golf with world number one Greg Norman, arrived at a tropical Australian resort on Thursday for two days of swimming, snorkelling and, no doubt, more golf.
Clinton, the business end of the Australian leg of his Asian trip behind him, arrived at the luxury Sheraton Mirage resort with wife Hillary by U.S. Marine helicopter.

The resort, one of Australia's most expensive, features the Great Barrier Reef some 30 nautical miles offshore, and Clinton plans to snorkel on the reef on Friday after delivering a brief environment statement.

There will also be a chance to play golf or visit a rainforest in what's known as "downtime" -- a chance for the couple to recharge the batteries after a hectic re-election campaign and before next week's APEC summit in the Philippines.
The town of Port Douglas, population 2,500, is a hideaway for the rich and famous on the far northeast coast of Australia, in the northern state of Queensland.

Clinton's only public event on Thursday was a speech at a harbourside park in Sydney, 3,000 km (1,800 miles) to the south of Port Douglas, in which he took issue with anti-immigrant sentiment in the United States and Australia and argued that ethnic diversity was a source of strength and a cause for pride.

Speaking at a harbourside park with the soaring Sydney Opera House in the background, a tired, hoarse-sounding Clinton said Sydney's 2000 Summer Olympics would showcase the melting pot heritage that Australians and Americans share.
In a country that has given the U.S. president a very warm welcome, Clinton's speech got a peculiarly mute reception from a crowd of a few thousand people.

Race and immigration has become the subject of a sensitive national debate in Australia since a maverick politician, Pauline Hanson, complained in parliament in September that Australia was being swamped by Asians.
But Clinton portrayed Australia as a country of harmony.
"I cannot think of a better place in the entire world, a more shining example of how people can come together as one nation and one community than Sydney, Australia," he said.
"I'm so grateful that you'll be here for the Olympics in 2000," he said.
Otherwise, the day was devoted to jogging, sightseeing and the fulfilment of a duffer's dream -- a round of golf with Australian golf idol Greg Norman.
After jogging in the Royal Botanic Gardens in the centre of Sydney, the president made an impromptu stop at the landmark opera house and later went shopping with his wife Hillary.
But the most keenly-awaited event was a game of golf with world number one Norman, which had some potential for embarrassment, etiquette-wise as well as athletic.
During his re-election campaign, when he was riding high in the polls over Republican rival Bob Dole, Clinton regularly warned complacent aides: "Remember Greg Norman".

That was a reference to the fact that the world's greatest golfer went into the final round of April's U.S. Masters with a six-stroke lead only to lose by five strokes to Britain's Nick Faldo, burnishing his reputation as a "choker".
Clinton was asked how he felt as he was teeing off with the man known as the "Shark". "Terrified," he replied before hooking his first shot well to the left.
"It was pretty much an 18 hole golf lesson for President Clinton by Greg Norman. They didn't keep score," said a White House spokesman.

The Clintons will leave Australia on Saturday for the Philippines where the president will meet the leaders of China, Japan and South Korea and attend the one-day Asia-Pacific Ecomomic Cooperation (APEC) leaders' summit the next day.
